title: Ensure kubelet anonymous authentication is disabled
description: In Oracle OKE, this control means the kubelet on managed or self managed worker nodes must not accept unauthenticated requests. OKE worker nodes run kubelet to communicate with the cluster control plane, and kubelet behavior can be configured through supported worker node startup or provisioning configuration. Reads every node's effective kubelet configuration through the API server (kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz); requires kubectl with nodes/proxy access.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.2.1 Ensure kubelet anonymous authentication is disabled

audit.command:
nodes=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}') || exit 1
[ -n "$nodes" ] || exit 1
ok=1
for n in $nodes; do
  c=$(kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$n/proxy/configz") || exit 1
  if ! { printf '%s' "$c" | grep -Eq '"anonymous":\{"enabled":false\}'; }; then echo "noncompliant: $n"; ok=0; fi
done
if [ "$ok" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: If the audit returns true, the worker node is allowing anonymous requests to the kubelet and should be treated as noncompliant. If the result is null or the field is missing, first confirm the configz response is complete, because Kubernetes identifies that endpoint as the view of the kubelet’s final effective configuration. Once the result is validated, remediation in OKE should be performed through the supported worker node provisioning or node update workflow, not by directly editing the kubelet config file on the host. OKE supports custom cloud-init scripts for managed nodes, and the corrected setting should be applied by creating, cycling, or replacing worker nodes. Remediation of new cluster When creating a new OKE cluster or node pool, the goal is to ensure worker nodes join the cluster with kubelet anonymous authentication already disabled.

title: Ensure that the cluster-admin role is only used where required
description: Verify that cluster administrative access in Oracle OKE is granted only to identities with a documented need for full cluster administration. In OKE, this review should cover Kubernetes ClusterRoleBinding assignments to the cluster-admin ClusterRole, OCI IAM users or groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, and any service accounts bound to cluster administrative permissions. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.1 Ensure that the cluster-admin role is only used where required

audit.command: This audit reviews Kubernetes ClusterRoleBinding objects in the Oracle OKE cluster to identify principals that are directly granted the cluster-admin ClusterRole. It lists each matching binding and its associated users, groups, or service accounts so the reviewer can verify whether full cluster administrative access is justified. Because OKE uses OCI IAM for access to OKE and the cluster control plane, and Kubernetes RBAC for cluster authorization, this check should be used as a partial review of administrative privilege rather than the sole test of cluster-admin exposure.

remediation.command: Review each ClusterRoleBinding identified by the audit that grants the Kubernetes cluster-admin ClusterRole, and determine whether the listed user, group, or service account still requires full cluster administrative access. In Oracle OKE, this review should also account for access granted through OCI IAM policies and Kubernetes RBAC mappings, because Oracle documents that IAM and the Kubernetes RBAC Authorizer work together to authorize Kubernetes operations. Where responsibilities are limited to a namespace, workload, or operational function, replace cluster administration with a narrower authorization model. • Review each principal returned by the audit and confirm whether full cluster administrative access is still justified for that identity.

title: Minimize the admission of privileged containers
description: Minimize the admission of privileged containers in OKE by enforcing Pod Security Standards through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine, and restrict privileged workloads to only the limited system or platform namespaces that truly require them. Do not generally permit containers to run with securityContext.privileged: true in OKE clusters, except for narrowly approved system or platform workloads. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.2.1 Minimize the admission of privileged containers

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$ns:=.metadata.namespace}}{{$p:=.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.containers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.privileged}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.initContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.privileged}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.ephemeralContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.privileged}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($4=="true")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Configure Pod Security Admission on workload namespaces so privileged containers are denied when new pods are created. For this control, both baseline and restricted disallow privileged containers, but restricted is typically the stronger choice for user workloads. Only enforce blocks noncompliant pods. warn and audit are useful during rollout, but they do not remediate the issue by themselves. Label each workload namespace to enforce restricted. kubectl label ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite Add warn and audit labels during transition so violations are surfaced before or alongside enforcement.

title: Use OCI IAM or OIDC tokens instead of user client certificates
description: OKE authenticates cluster users through OCI IAM by default, and enhanced clusters can also be configured to use an external OIDC identity provider for user authentication. User access should rely on OCI IAM or OIDC tokens rather than Kubernetes client certificates, because these mechanisms align user access to managed identity, policy, and RBAC controls. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 2.1.1 Use OCI IAM or OIDC tokens instead of user client certificates

audit.command: Review user access to the cluster and ensure that users are not making use of Kubernetes client certificate authentication. Review approved user kubeconfig files and confirm that user entries use OCI IAM generated tokens or OIDC tokens instead of client certificate fields. Run the following command to verify the authentication method configured for users in the current kubeconfig file: kubectl config view --raw -o json | jq -r ' .users[] | [ .name, ( if .user.exec then "exec_token" elif .user["auth-provider"]?.name == "oidc" then "oidc_token" elif .user.token then "static_token" ...

remediation.command: Replace user kubeconfig entries that use client certificates with OCI IAM generated tokens or OIDC token based authentication. For OKE clusters, user authentication should align to the supported OKE access model, where OCI IAM is used by default and OIDC can be configured for external identity provider based authentication. This allows user access to be managed through identity, policy, and Kubernetes RBAC controls rather than long lived certificate material stored in kubeconfig files. • For OCI IAM based access, regenerate the user kubeconfig file from OKE using kubeconfig token version 2.0.0 so the user entry uses the OCI CLI exec plugin to generate authentication tokens. • For OIDC based access, configure the OKE cluster for OIDC authentication and update the user kubeconfig entry to use the approved OIDC identity provider token flow.

title: Ensure authorized access to OCI Audit logs for OKE activity
description: OCI Audit logs are separate from OKE managed Kubernetes control plane service logs. OKE integrates with the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Audit service to record operations performed by Kubernetes Engine and the Kubernetes API server as Audit log events. Operations performed by Kubernetes Engine and the Kubernetes API server are visible as log events in the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Audit service. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 2.2.1 Ensure authorized access to OCI Audit logs for OKE activity

audit.command: To monitor and manage operations performed by Container Engine for Kubernetes on a particular cluster: Review IAM policies and confirm that only authorized groups are granted access to read OCI Audit events for the tenancy or approved compartment. The read audit-events permission allows access to Audit log events. To view operations performed by Container Engine for Kubernetes and the Kubernetes API server as log events in the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Audit service: Open the navigation menu, select Identity & Security, and then select Audit.

remediation.command: Update OCI IAM policies so only approved security, operations, or audit groups can read OCI Audit events for the required tenancy or compartment. Remove broad or unnecessary Audit access from users or groups that do not require it, and validate that authorized users can view OKE related events in the Audit service using the appropriate compartment and filters.

title: Ensure kubelet authorization mode is set to Webhook
description: In OKE, the available kubelet authorization modes are AlwaysAllow and Webhook. For worker nodes, the recommended setting is Webhook, which uses the Kubernetes authorization flow to evaluate access to the kubelet API. In contrast, AlwaysAllow is not optimal because it bypasses that authorization decision and permits kubelet requests without a webhook-based access check. Reads every node's effective kubelet configuration through the API server (kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz); requires kubectl with nodes/proxy access.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.2.2 Ensure kubelet authorization mode is set to Webhook

audit.command:
nodes=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}') || exit 1
[ -n "$nodes" ] || exit 1
ok=1
for n in $nodes; do
  c=$(kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$n/proxy/configz") || exit 1
  if ! { printf '%s' "$c" | grep -Eq '"authorization":\{"mode":"Webhook"'; }; then echo "noncompliant: $n"; ok=0; fi
done
if [ "$ok" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: If the audit returns AlwaysAllow, the worker node is permitting kubelet requests without webhook-based authorization and should be treated as noncompliant. If the result is null or the field is missing, first confirm the configz response is complete, because Kubernetes identifies that endpoint as the view of the kubelet’s final actuated configuration. Once the result is validated, remediation in OKE should be performed through the supported worker node initialization, node pool update, or node replacement workflow, not by directly editing the kubelet config file on the host. Oracle documents that OKE managed nodes can use custom cloud-init initialization scripts, that the OKE default logic should not be modified, and that worker node property changes apply to new worker nodes.

title: Ensure the kubelet X.509 client CA file is configured
description: This setting in OKE is about configuring the kubelet with a trusted X.509 client CA source so the kubelet can validate client certificates presented to its HTTPS endpoint. It is not the same as validating the kubelet’s own serving certificate from the API server side. In OKE, kubelet authentication settings should be evaluated in the effective kubelet configuration applied during managed node initialization. Reads every node's effective kubelet configuration through the API server (kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz); requires kubectl with nodes/proxy access.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.2.3 Ensure the kubelet X.509 client CA file is configured

audit.command:
nodes=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}') || exit 1
[ -n "$nodes" ] || exit 1
ok=1
for n in $nodes; do
  c=$(kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$n/proxy/configz") || exit 1
  if ! { printf '%s' "$c" | grep -Eq '"clientCAFile":"[^"]+"'; }; then echo "noncompliant: $n"; ok=0; fi
done
if [ "$ok" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: If the audit shows that the kubelet X.509 client CA file is not configured, the worker node should be treated as noncompliant. If the result is empty, null, or missing, first confirm the inspection reflects the effective node configuration. In OKE, remediation should be performed through the supported managed node initialization, node pool update, or node replacement workflow, because Oracle supports custom cloud-init initialization scripts for managed nodes and updated node pool properties are applied when replacement managed nodes are started. Remediation of new cluster When creating a new OKE cluster or node group, the goal is to ensure each worker node starts with a trusted client CA bundle already present and with the kubelet configured to use it for certificate-based client authentication.

title: Ensure the kubelet read-only port is disabled
description: In OKE, this setting is intended to keep kubelet access limited to the standard secured management path used for node operations, instead of exposing an additional legacy interface on the worker node. In practice, it should be assessed in the node’s effective kubelet configuration because OKE applies managed node behavior through cloud-init initialization, node pool configuration, and worker node replacement workflows rather than relying only on ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.2.4 Ensure the kubelet read-only port is disabled

audit.command: To audit whether the kubelet read-only port is disabled on an OKE worker node, query the live effective kubelet configuration through the Kubernetes API server proxy and inspect the kubelet configz output for readOnlyPort set to 0. Kubernetes identifies configz as the view of the kubelet’s final actuated configuration, and the kubelet configuration schema defines readOnlyPort as the setting that controls the unauthenticated read-only kubelet service.

remediation.command: If the audit returns a nonzero readOnlyPort``, the worker node is exposing the kubelet read-only service and should be treated as noncompliant. If the field is missing from configz, first confirm whether it is simply omitted because the effective value is 0, since the kubelet configuration schema defines readOnlyPortas the unauthenticated read-only service and states that0` disables it. Once a noncompliant state is confirmed, remediation in OKE should be performed through the supported managed node initialization, node pool update, or node replacement workflow, not by directly editing the kubelet config file on the host. Oracle documents that OKE managed nodes use cloud-init initialization scripts, that custom logic can be added without modifying the default OKE initialization logic, and that updated worker node properties are applied by starting replacement worker nodes.

title: Ensure kubelet tlsCertFile and tlsPrivateKeyFile are configured appropriately
description: Setup TLS connection on the Kubelets. For OKE worker nodes, this control validates that the kubelet HTTPS serving endpoint uses an appropriate TLS certificate and private key configuration rather than relying on an unintended or unmanaged serving identity. Reads every node's effective kubelet configuration through the API server (kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz); requires kubectl with nodes/proxy access.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.2.7 Ensure kubelet tlsCertFile and tlsPrivateKeyFile are configured appropriately

audit.command:
nodes=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}') || exit 1
[ -n "$nodes" ] || exit 1
ok=1
for n in $nodes; do
  c=$(kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$n/proxy/configz") || exit 1
  if ! { printf '%s' "$c" | grep -Eq '"tlsCertFile":"[^"]+"' && printf '%s' "$c" | grep -Eq '"tlsPrivateKeyFile":"[^"]+"'; }; then echo "noncompliant: $n"; ok=0; fi
done
if [ "$ok" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: If the audit shows that the kubelet serving certificate and private key are not configured appropriately, first confirm the inspection reflects the effective node configuration. In OKE, remediation should be performed through the supported managed node initialization, node pool update, or node replacement workflow, not by directly editing the kubelet config file on the host. Oracle supports custom cloud-init initialization scripts for managed nodes, including kubelet extra args, and updated worker node properties are applied through new or replacement worker nodes. Remediation of new cluster When creating a new OKE cluster or node pool, ensure each worker node starts with the intended kubelet serving certificate and private key configuration. If customization is required, place the certificate, private key, and kubelet reference in the supported managed node initialization path.

title: Ensure the kubelet client certificate rotation is enabled
description: In OKE, the setting rotateCertificates is about whether the kubelet renews its client certificate before that certificate expires. Oracle OKE documentation shows worker nodes using the kubelet client certificate at /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem, which is trusted by the cluster CA, but Oracle does not publish a fixed OKE default for rotateCertificates. Reads every node's effective kubelet configuration through the API server (kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz); requires kubectl with nodes/proxy access.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.2.8 Ensure the kubelet client certificate rotation is enabled

audit.command:
nodes=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}') || exit 1
[ -n "$nodes" ] || exit 1
ok=1
for n in $nodes; do
  c=$(kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$n/proxy/configz") || exit 1
  if ! { printf '%s' "$c" | grep -Eq '"rotateCertificates":true'; }; then echo "noncompliant: $n"; ok=0; fi
done
if [ "$ok" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: If the audit returns false, the worker node is not configured to rotate its kubelet client certificate and should be treated as noncompliant. If the field is not present, interpret that conservatively as rotation not enabled unless your OKE platform explicitly manages certificate rotation for you. Oracle OKE documentation shows worker nodes using kubelet client certificates trusted by the cluster CA and supports managed node customization through cloud-init initialization scripts and kubelet extra args. Oracle also documents that worker node property changes can be applied through new or replacement managed nodes. Remediation of new cluster When creating a new OKE cluster or node pool, the goal is to ensure worker nodes start with kubelet client certificate rotation enabled if the nodes may remain in service long enough for certificate expiry to matter.

title: Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required
description: Verify that access to Kubernetes Secret objects in Oracle OKE is granted only to OCI IAM users or groups, Kubernetes users or groups, and service accounts with a defined operational or workload need. The review should cover OCI IAM access to the cluster, Kubernetes RBAC roles and bindings, OCI IAM groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, workload identities, and service account permissions, with particular attention to permissions that allow get, ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.2 Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required

audit.command: Start by reviewing every path that can grant access to Kubernetes Secret objects in the OKE cluster. Start with OCI IAM access to the cluster and Kubernetes RBAC permissions, because OKE uses OCI IAM to control access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls cluster authorization. Then review Kubernetes RBAC, service account permissions, and workload identities, because OKE can combine cluster access, Kubernetes RBAC, and OCI resource access through service account based workload identity.

remediation.command: Start by reducing every access path that allows reading Kubernetes Secret objects in the OKE cluster. Start with OCI IAM access and Kubernetes RBAC permissions, because OCI IAM controls access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls access to Kubernetes resources such as Secrets. Then reduce unnecessary access in Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, and workload identity policies, and replace broad permissions with the narrowest namespace or workload scope that still supports the required function. • Remove or narrow OCI IAM and Kubernetes RBAC permissions that expose Secrets, and prefer namespace access over cluster scope wherever possible. • Replace broad RBAC permissions on secrets with the smallest practical Role or ClusterRole, and remove unnecessary get, list, or watch access from users, groups, and service accounts.

title: Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used.
description: Default service accounts in OKE should not be used as the active identity for ordinary application or automation workloads. If a Pod does not specify a service account, Kubernetes automatically assigns the namespace default service account, and that account can authenticate to the Kubernetes API through its mounted token. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Fails when a default service account does not set automountServiceAccountToken: false or is bound to a Role/ClusterRole.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.5 Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used.

audit.command:
sa=$(kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{if eq .metadata.name "default"}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.automountServiceAccountToken}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
rb=$(kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$b:=.metadata.name}}{{$bn:=.metadata.namespace}}{{range .subjects}}{{if eq .kind "ServiceAccount"}}{{if eq .name "default"}}{{if .namespace}}{{.namespace}}{{else}}{{$bn}}{{end}} {{$b}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$sa" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && $2!="false" {print "automount: " $1}')
bad2=$(printf '%s
' "$rb" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex {print "binding: " $0}')
if [ -z "$bad$bad2" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
%s
' "$bad" "$bad2" | grep . | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Create dedicated service accounts for workloads that need Kubernetes API access or OKE workload identity, and update those workloads to explicitly set serviceAccountName rather than relying on the namespace default service account. For workloads that do not need Kubernetes API access, disable service account token auto mounting and avoid using the default service account as the active workload identity. Also review the default service account in each namespace and ensure it is not bound to unnecessary RBAC permissions. Modify the default service account in each application namespace to set: automountServiceAccountToken: false Then validate workload manifests, because a Pod automountServiceAccountToken setting can override the service account setting, and workloads that actually need Kubernetes API access must use an explicitly assigned service account instead of inheriting default.

title: Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted where necessary
description: Service account tokens in OKE should be mounted only for Pods that require Kubernetes API access or an explicitly configured workload identity flow. Kubernetes supports disabling automatic token mounting at the Pod or ServiceAccount level, and workloads that need OCI access through OKE workload identity should use a dedicated service account rather than relying on broad default token mounting. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Reports pods with an auto-mounted service account token (kube-api-access-* volume).
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.6 Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted where necessary

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.volumes}} {{.name}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($0 ~ / kube-api-access-/)')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Apply the following steps to reduce unnecessary service account token mounting in OKE: • Set automountServiceAccountToken to false for Pods and ServiceAccounts that do not require Kubernetes API access. This reduces unnecessary default token auto mounting. • Update workloads to use a dedicated serviceAccountName only where a service account token is operationally required, instead of inheriting token behavior from the namespace default service account. Each application should use its own dedicated service account. • For workloads that need OCI access, use OKE workload identity with a dedicated service account rather than broad default token mounting. OKE workload identity uses the combination of cluster, namespace, and service account to grant access to OCI resources for the intended workload.

title: Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host process ID namespace
description: Minimize the admission of pods that request host process ID namespace sharing by restricting use of spec.hostPID: true in OKE workload namespaces. In the OKE Pod Security Standards model, this is enforced through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine. Because the baseline profile prohibits hostPID and restricted inherits that restriction, general user workloads should not be permitted to use host PID sharing. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.2.2 Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host process ID namespace

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}} {{.spec.hostPID}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($3=="true")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Configure Pod Security Admission on workload namespaces so pods that request spec.hostPID: true are denied at admission time. For this control, the baseline and restricted Pod Security Standards disallow hostPID, while restricted is typically the stronger choice for user workloads. For remediation, use enforce because only enforce rejects violating pods. warn and audit can help during rollout, but they do not block admission. Label each workload namespace to enforce restricted. kubectl label ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite Add warn and audit during transition if you want visibility into violations before or alongside enforcement.

In the OKE Pod Security Standards model, this is done through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.2.3 Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host IPC namespace

title: Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host network namespace
description: Minimize the admission of pods that request spec.hostNetwork: true in OKE so that sharing the host network namespace is limited to tightly controlled, explicitly approved platform scenarios. In OKE, this is done through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine. Because the baseline profile prohibits hostNetwork, and restricted inherits the baseline restrictions, general workload namespaces should not permit host network sharing. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.2.4 Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host network namespace

"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($3=="true")')

remediation.command: Configure Pod Security Admission on workload namespaces so pods that request spec.hostNetwork: true are denied at admission time. Use enforce on workload namespaces with restricted, or at minimum baseline, and reserve any exceptions for narrowly approved platform workloads. After updating namespace enforcement, remove hostNetwork: true from affected manifests and redeploy those workloads so new pods are evaluated under the enforced policy. For this control, the baseline and restricted Pod Security Standards disallow hostNetwork, while restricted is typically the stronger choice for user workloads. Label each workload namespace to enforce restricted. kubectl label ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite Add warn and audit during rollout if you want visibility into violations, but do not rely on them for remediation because they do not block pod creation.

title: Minimize the admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation
description: Minimize the admission of containers with securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: true in OKE so that general workload namespaces do not permit processes to gain more privileges than their parent process. In OKE, this should be enforced through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Containers that do not explicitly set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false are reported.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.2.5 Minimize the admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$ns:=.metadata.namespace}}{{$p:=.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.containers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.allowPrivilegeEscalation}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.initContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.allowPrivilegeEscalation}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.ephemeralContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.allowPrivilegeEscalation}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($4!="false")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Configure Pod Security Admission on workload namespaces so containers that do not explicitly set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false are denied at admission time. In OKE, use restricted for workload namespaces, or an equivalent policy engine, because restricted requires allowPrivilegeEscalation=false. Use enforce for actual remediation, since warn and audit only report violations and do not block pod creation. Label each workload namespace to enforce restricted. kubectl label ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite Add warn and audit during rollout if you want visibility into violations before or alongside enforcement.

title: Prefer exposing secrets as mounted files rather than environment variables
description: Secrets for OKE workloads are better exposed as mounted files than as environment variables. Kubernetes secrets can be consumed either way, and Oracle supports mounting secrets from OCI Vault into Kubernetes Pods through the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Reports containers using env valueFrom.secretKeyRef or envFrom.secretRef.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.4.1 Prefer exposing secrets as mounted files rather than environment variables

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$ns:=.metadata.namespace}}{{$p:=.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.containers}}{{$c:=.name}}{{range .env}}{{if .valueFrom}}{{if .valueFrom.secretKeyRef}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{$c}} env{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{range .envFrom}}{{if .secretRef}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{$c}} envFrom{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{range .spec.initContainers}}{{$c:=.name}}{{range .env}}{{if .valueFrom}}{{if .valueFrom.secretKeyRef}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{$c}} env{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{range .envFrom}}{{if .secretRef}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{$c}} envFrom{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && (1)')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Update workloads to consume secrets as mounted files instead of environment variables. Replace env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef and envFrom[].secretRef usage with Kubernetes Secret volumes or the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, then update the application to read the secret from the mounted file path. This reduces the chance of secret values appearing in logs and aligns with the OCI Vault based file delivery pattern for OKE workloads. Replace secret environment variables with mounted secret files and update the application to read from the mounted path.

title: Consider external secret storage
description: External secret storage for OKE means keeping application secrets outside native Kubernetes Secret objects and retrieving them from a managed service such as OCI Vault when workloads need them. This approach lets OKE workloads consume secrets through integrations such as the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, instead of relying only on Kubernetes to store and distribute sensitive values. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.4.2 Consider external secret storage

audit.command: Review the OKE cluster’s secrets architecture and verify that required workloads use an external secrets store such as OCI Vault instead of relying only on native Kubernetes Secret objects. The audit should confirm both the integration path and the workload access model, because external secret storage in OKE typically depends on the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider, the Secrets Store CSI Driver, and OCI IAM access through OKE workload identity.

remediation.command: Move sensitive application secrets out of native Kubernetes Secret objects and into an external store such as OCI Vault. Then update OKE workloads to retrieve those secrets through the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, using OCI IAM access through OKE workload identity. This shifts encryption, access control, rotation, and auditing to OCI instead of leaving those functions primarily in Secret objects stored inside the cluster. • Create the required secrets in OCI Vault and define workload access with least privilege OCI IAM policies. • Install and configure the OCI Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider and the Secrets Store CSI Driver for OKE. • Update workload manifests to mount external secrets through a SecretProviderClass instead of reading only native Kubernetes Secret objects.

title: Use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for OKE workloads
description: Using dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for OKE workloads helps isolate OCI permissions by application, job, or trust boundary instead of sharing a single identity across multiple workloads. This supports more controlled access to OCI services and reduces the security impact if one workload is compromised or misconfigured. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Reports pods running as the namespace default service account.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.2.1 Use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for OKE workloads

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}} {{.spec.serviceAccountName}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($3=="default" || $3=="<no")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for OKE workloads and associate OCI permissions to those service accounts instead of relying on the namespace default service account or broad node based OCI permissions. Use OKE workload identity for workloads that need OCI resource access. Create one dedicated service account and OCI IAM policy design for each application or distinct permission boundary, and update workload manifests to reference the intended service account explicitly. Disable automatic service account token mounting for workloads that do not need Kubernetes API access. After migrating workloads to dedicated service accounts, restrict access to node or instance principal credentials where applicable so pods cannot inherit broader node credentials.

title: Use customer managed KMS keys for OKE envelope encryption of Kubernetes secrets
description: Using customer managed OCI Vault keys for OKE Kubernetes secrets encryption adds a customer managed protection layer for Kubernetes secrets stored through the Kubernetes API. This strengthens data at rest protection while allowing organizations to manage key ownership, rotation, policy, and audit visibility for the key used to protect secret data. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.3.1 Use customer managed KMS keys for OKE envelope encryption of Kubernetes secrets

audit.command: Review the OKE cluster configuration and verify that Kubernetes secrets are protected with a customer managed OCI Vault key, not only the default Oracle managed encryption for the block volumes used by etcd. For this control, the important check is whether the cluster is associated with a customer managed key for Kubernetes secrets encryption. Also verify that the key is usable by the cluster and has not been disabled, deleted, or stripped of required permissions.

remediation.command: Configure the OKE cluster to use a customer managed OCI Vault key for envelope encryption of Kubernetes secrets so secret data stored through the Kubernetes API is protected with a customer managed master encryption key. This requires an existing master encryption key in OCI Vault, with policy permissions that allow OKE clusters to use the key. OKE does not allow you to enable customer managed Kubernetes secrets encryption on an existing cluster after creation. Oracle documents that this option is selected when creating a new cluster through the Custom Create workflow or with the OCI CLI by specifying the Vault key OCID. • After the new cluster is created, the key must remain enabled and accessible. Disabling, deleting, or breaking access to the associated key can place the cluster in a degraded or unrecoverable state.

title: Restrict OKE control plane endpoint access using private endpoints or approved CIDRs
description: This recommendation is about reducing exposure of the Kubernetes API server without necessarily making it private only. The intended end state is that the OKE Kubernetes API endpoint is placed behind a private endpoint where possible, or if a public IP address is assigned, access is limited to approved source CIDRs through OCI network security rules. Reported as a manual review because it needs site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.1 Restrict OKE control plane endpoint access using private endpoints or approved CIDRs

audit.command: Check the OKE Kubernetes API endpoint configuration and determine whether the endpoint has a public IP address assigned. Also identify the endpoint subnet and any network security groups attached to the endpoint. oci ce cluster get \ --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID \ --query 'data.{endpointConfig:"endpoint-config",endpoints:endpoints}' \ --output json Expected Output: { "endpointConfig": { "is-public-ip-enabled": false, "nsg-ids": [ "ocid1.networksecuritygroup.oc1..." ], "subnet-id": "ocid1.subnet.oc1..." }, "endpoints": { "private-endpoint": "10.0.0.10:6443", "public-endpoint": null } } ...

remediation.command: Restrict access to the OKE Kubernetes API endpoint by using a private endpoint where possible, or by limiting public endpoint access through OCI network security groups or security lists. The Kubernetes API endpoint is hosted in a VCN subnet, and Oracle recommends using network security groups or security lists to control access to that subnet. For new clusters, place the Kubernetes API endpoint in a private subnet when internet access to the API endpoint is not required.

title: Enable private OKE control plane access and disable public IP access
description: This recommendation is the strict private access version of API endpoint hardening. The intended end state is that the Kubernetes API server is reachable only from inside the cluster VCN or from a connected private network, and there is no internet-reachable public API endpoint at all. This is a pure control plane exposure decision. Requires the oci CLI with read access to the cluster in OKE_CLUSTER_ID.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.2 Enable private OKE control plane access and disable public IP access

audit.command:
pub=$(oci ce cluster get --cluster-id "${OKE_CLUSTER_ID:?set OKE_CLUSTER_ID}" --query 'data."endpoint-config"."is-public-ip-enabled"' --raw-output) || exit 1
ep=$(oci ce cluster get --cluster-id "${OKE_CLUSTER_ID:?set OKE_CLUSTER_ID}" --query 'data.endpoints."public-endpoint"' --raw-output) || exit 1
if [ "$pub" = false ] && { [ -z "$ep" ] || [ "$ep" = null ]; }; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: is-public-ip-enabled=$pub public-endpoint=$ep"; fi

remediation.command: Use private OKE control plane access by placing the Kubernetes API endpoint in a private subnet and disabling public IP assignment. This keeps Kubernetes API access on the VCN or an approved private network path. For a new cluster, create the Kubernetes API endpoint in a private subnet and do not assign a public IP address. oci ce cluster create \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --compartment-id $COMPARTMENT_ID \ --vcn-id $VCN_OCID \ --kubernetes-version $KUBERNETES_VERSION \ --endpoint-subnet-id $PRIVATE_ENDPOINT_SUBNET_OCID \ --endpoint-public-ip-enabled false For an existing cluster, update the endpoint configuration so the Kubernetes API endpoint is not assigned a public IP address.

title: Ensure clusters are created with Private Nodes
description: This recommendation is about the data plane, not the control plane. It means worker nodes are placed in private subnets and are not intended to have direct public internet exposure. In the common pattern, nodes run in private subnets while internet-facing ingress resources are placed in public subnets. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.3 Ensure clusters are created with Private Nodes

audit.command: Review the subnets used by each OKE node pool and verify that worker nodes are deployed in private subnets, not public subnets. For this control, the deciding evidence is node subnet placement, public IP behavior, and subnet routing, not the control plane endpoint settings. A compliant private-node design places nodes in subnets that prohibit public IP assignment on VNICs and do not have a default route to an Internet Gateway. If outbound access is required, the design should use a NAT gateway, service gateway, or other required private network path instead.

remediation.command: For existing worker nodes that run in public subnets, remediate the nodes by replacing them with a new node pool that uses only private subnets, then migrating workloads and retiring the original node pool. The target private subnets should prohibit public IP assignment on VNICs and should not have a default route to an Internet Gateway. If outbound access is required for image pulls or OCI API calls, provide it through a NAT gateway, service gateway, or the required private network path instead. • Create a new node pool that uses only private subnet IDs. Do not reuse public subnets for the replacement worker nodes. • Ensure the replacement subnets prohibit public IP assignment on VNICs, so new worker instances are launched without public IPs. • Ensure the route tables for those subnets do not send 0.0.0.0/0 directly to an Internet Gateway.

title: Use TLS certificates on OKE load balancer listeners for encrypted client connections
description: Using TLS certificates on OKE load balancer listeners protects client to load balancer traffic in transit by presenting a trusted server certificate and negotiating encrypted HTTPS or TLS connections at the listener. In OKE, this commonly means configuring TLS on an OCI Load Balancer created for Kubernetes Service resources, or configuring HTTPS/TLS on OCI native ingress controller listeners so externally exposed application entry points do not ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.5 Use TLS certificates on OKE load balancer listeners for encrypted client connections

audit.command: Review all OKE Service resources of type LoadBalancer and all Ingress resources that expose client traffic, and verify that client facing listeners use HTTPS or TLS with a valid certificate. For OCI Load Balancer backed Service resources, listener encryption is configured with annotations such as service.beta.kubernetes.io/oci-load-balancer-ssl-ports and service.beta.kubernetes.io/oci-load-balancer-tls-secret, or with OCI Certificates based configuration where used.

remediation.command: Configure every client facing OKE load balancer listener to use HTTPS or TLS with a valid certificate so client to load balancer traffic is encrypted in transit. For OCI Load Balancer backed Service resources, configure SSL/TLS listener ports and associate a TLS certificate using Kubernetes secrets or OCI Certificates based configuration. For OCI native ingress controller resources, configure HTTPS/TLS listeners and associate the required Kubernetes secret or certificate OCID. If the design requires encryption beyond the load balancer, implement backend TLS separately because listener TLS alone protects only the client facing connection. • Add a valid certificate to each client facing OCI Load Balancer or OCI native ingress controller listener that should serve encrypted traffic.

title: Ensure that the kubelet.conf file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive
description: If kubelet is running, and if it is using a file-based kubelet.conf file, ensure that the proxy kubelet.conf file has permissions of 644 or more restrictive. Runs on each OKE worker node (path from the kubelet argument).
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.1.1 Ensure that the kubelet.conf file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive

audit.command:
set -f
psarg() { ps -eo args 2>/dev/null | grep -E "^([^ ]*/)?$1( |\$)" | head -n 1 | awk -v k="--$2" '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++){if($i==k&&i<NF)v=$(i+1); else if(index($i,k"=")==1)v=substr($i,length(k)+2)}} END{if(v!="")print v}'; }
p0=$(psarg kubelet kubeconfig)
f=""; for x in ${p0:-} /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf; do if [ -e "$x" ]; then f=$x; break; fi; done
[ -n "$f" ] || exit 1
p=$(stat -Lc %a "$f") || exit 1
if [ $((0$p & 0133)) -eq 0 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: $f mode $p"; fi

remediation.guidance: Run the below command (based on the file location on your system) on the each worker node. For example, chmod 644 <kubelet.conf file>

title: Ensure that the kubelet.conf file ownership is set to root:root
description: If kubelet is running, ensure that the file ownership of its kubelet.conf file is set to root:root. Runs on each OKE worker node (path from the kubelet argument).
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.1.2 Ensure that the kubelet.conf file ownership is set to root:root

audit.command:
set -f
psarg() { ps -eo args 2>/dev/null | grep -E "^([^ ]*/)?$1( |\$)" | head -n 1 | awk -v k="--$2" '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++){if($i==k&&i<NF)v=$(i+1); else if(index($i,k"=")==1)v=substr($i,length(k)+2)}} END{if(v!="")print v}'; }
p0=$(psarg kubelet kubeconfig)
f=""; for x in ${p0:-} /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf; do if [ -e "$x" ]; then f=$x; break; fi; done
[ -n "$f" ] || exit 1
o=$(stat -Lc %U:%G "$f") || exit 1
if [ "$o" = "root:root" ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: $f $o"; fi

remediation.guidance: Run the below command (based on the file location on your system) on the each worker node. For example, chown root:root <kubelet.conf file>

title: Ensure that the kubelet configuration file has permissions set to 644 or more restrictive
description: Ensure that if the kubelet refers to a configuration file with the --config argument, that file has permissions of 644 or more restrictive. Runs on each OKE worker node (path from the kubelet argument).
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.1.3 Ensure that the kubelet configuration file has permissions set to 644 or more restrictive

audit.command:
set -f
psarg() { ps -eo args 2>/dev/null | grep -E "^([^ ]*/)?$1( |\$)" | head -n 1 | awk -v k="--$2" '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++){if($i==k&&i<NF)v=$(i+1); else if(index($i,k"=")==1)v=substr($i,length(k)+2)}} END{if(v!="")print v}'; }
p0=$(psarg kubelet config)
f=""; for x in ${p0:-} /etc/kubernetes/kubelet-config.json; do if [ -e "$x" ]; then f=$x; break; fi; done
[ -n "$f" ] || exit 1
p=$(stat -Lc %a "$f") || exit 1
if [ $((0$p & 0133)) -eq 0 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: $f mode $p"; fi

remediation.guidance: Run the below command (based on the file location on your system) on the each worker node. For example, chmod 644 <kubelet-config.json file>

title: Ensure that the kubelet configuration file ownership is set to root:root
description: Ensure that if the kubelet refers to a configuration file with the --config argument, that file is owned by root:root. Runs on each OKE worker node (path from the kubelet argument).
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.1.4 Ensure that the kubelet configuration file ownership is set to root:root

audit.command:
set -f
psarg() { ps -eo args 2>/dev/null | grep -E "^([^ ]*/)?$1( |\$)" | head -n 1 | awk -v k="--$2" '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++){if($i==k&&i<NF)v=$(i+1); else if(index($i,k"=")==1)v=substr($i,length(k)+2)}} END{if(v!="")print v}'; }
p0=$(psarg kubelet config)
f=""; for x in ${p0:-} /etc/kubernetes/kubelet-config.json; do if [ -e "$x" ]; then f=$x; break; fi; done
[ -n "$f" ] || exit 1
o=$(stat -Lc %U:%G "$f") || exit 1
if [ "$o" = "root:root" ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: $f $o"; fi
