title: Ensure kubelet makeIPTablesUtilChains is set to true
description: This control is intended to keep kubelet-managed iptables support enabled on worker nodes so the node maintains the expected networking behavior for Kubernetes traffic handling. The recommended state is makeIPTablesUtilChains: true, and in OKE this should be enforced through the node’s managed initialization and node pool configuration, because OKE applies managed node customization through cloud-init initialization scripts, kubelet extra args, ... Reads every node's effective kubelet configuration through the API server (kubectl get --raw /api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz); requires kubectl with nodes/proxy access. A missing makeIPTablesUtilChains means the default (true).
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.2.5 Ensure kubelet makeIPTablesUtilChains is set to true

audit.command:
nodes=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}') || exit 1
[ -n "$nodes" ] || exit 1
ok=1
for n in $nodes; do
  c=$(kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$n/proxy/configz") || exit 1
  if ! { ! printf '%s' "$c" | grep -Eq '"makeIPTablesUtilChains":false'; }; then echo "noncompliant: $n"; ok=0; fi
done
if [ "$ok" -eq 1 ]; then echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: If the audit returns false, the worker node is not keeping kubelet iptables utility chains enabled and should be treated as noncompliant. If the result is null or the field is missing, first confirm the configz response is complete, because Kubernetes identifies that endpoint as the view of the kubelet’s final actuated configuration, and the kubelet configuration schema defines makeIPTablesUtilChains with a default of true. Once the result is validated, remediation in OKE should be performed through the supported managed node initialization, node pool update, or node replacement workflow, not by directly editing the kubelet config file on the host.

title: Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles
description: Verify that Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole objects in Oracle OKE do not use wildcard entries such as * for verbs, resources, or apiGroups unless a documented administrative or platform requirement exists. The review should also include the RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects that assign those roles to users, groups, or service accounts, because OKE uses OCI IAM to control access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.3 Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles

audit.command: Begin by reviewing custom Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole objects in OKE to identify any use of wildcard entries such as * for verbs, resources, or apiGroups. In OKE, this review should cover native RBAC objects, OCI IAM users and groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, workload identities, and Oracle managed platform RBAC objects that should be distinguished from customer managed permissions.

remediation.command: Start by replacing wildcard permissions in custom Role and ClusterRole objects with explicitly enumerated verbs, resources, and apiGroups that match the approved operational need. In OKE, this remediation should focus on customer managed RBAC objects, the bindings that assign them, OCI IAM users and groups mapped through Kubernetes RBAC, workload identities, and service accounts used by workloads or cluster components. OKE uses OCI IAM for access to OKE and the cluster control plane, and Kubernetes RBAC for authorization inside the cluster, so both access paths should be reviewed when excessive permissions are found. • Replace wildcard values in custom Role and ClusterRole rules with the specific verbs, resources, and apiGroups the function actually requires.

title: Minimize access to create pods
description: The ability to create Pods in OKE is a sensitive permission that should be limited to approved deployment and operational functions. In OKE, Pod creation is controlled through Kubernetes RBAC after OCI IAM allows access to the cluster control plane. Because Pods run within a namespace, use a service account, and can carry workload permissions, Pod creation should be limited to the smallest practical namespace and workload boundary. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.1.4 Minimize access to create pods

audit.command: Begin by reviewing every path that can grant the ability to create Pods in OKE. Start with OCI IAM access to the cluster and Kubernetes RBAC permissions, because OCI IAM controls access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls authorization inside the cluster. Then review Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, and Pod security controls, because Pod creation can allow an identity to launch workloads under available service accounts and potentially exercise both Kubernetes and OCI permissions.

remediation.command: Start by reducing every access path that allows Pod creation in OKE. Start with OCI IAM access and Kubernetes RBAC permissions, because OCI IAM controls access to OKE and the cluster control plane, while Kubernetes RBAC controls access to Kubernetes resources such as Pods. Then reduce unnecessary permissions in Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, and Pod security controls so Pod creation is limited to approved deployment paths and the smallest practical workload boundary. • Remove or narrow OCI IAM and Kubernetes RBAC permissions that allow Pod creation, and prefer namespace limited access wherever possible. • Replace broad RBAC permissions on pods, deployments, daemonsets, statefulsets, jobs, and cronjobs with the smallest Role or ClusterRole that supports the approved function.

title: Ensure the OKE CNI add-on uses an Oracle supported version
description: There are a variety of CNI plugins available for Kubernetes. In OKE, the CNI plugin used for pod networking is an essential cluster add-on and should run an Oracle supported version that is compatible with the cluster’s Kubernetes version. Reported as a manual review because it needs site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.3.1 Ensure the OKE CNI add-on uses an Oracle supported version

audit.command: Review the documentation of the OKE CNI add-on in use by the cluster, and confirm that it is an Oracle supported version for the Kubernetes version running on the cluster. • List the cluster add-ons deployed on the cluster and identify the installed CNI plugin add-on version. oci ce cluster list-addons --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID • List the add-on versions supported for the Kubernetes version running on the cluster. oci ce addon-option list --kubernetes-version $KUBERNETES_VERSION • If you know the CNI add-on name shown by the cluster, narrow the supported version check to that add-on.

remediation.command: Update the OKE CNI add on to an Oracle supported version that is compatible with the cluster’s Kubernetes version. If automatic add on updates are enabled, confirm the cluster is running a supported Kubernetes version so compatible CNI updates can be applied. If a specific add on version is selected, verify that the selected version is supported for the cluster’s Kubernetes version and update it when Oracle publishes a newer supported version. For the OCI CNI plugin, apply updates using Oracle’s documented approach. The recommended approach is to provision new nodes so they receive CNI plugin pods running the latest supported CNI plugin version, then drain and remove nodes running older CNI plugin pods when appropriate.

title: Ensure workload namespaces have required NetworkPolicies defined
description: Use network policies to isolate traffic in your cluster network. For OKE, ensure workload namespaces have required NetworkPolicies defined and that the selected networking configuration supports NetworkPolicy enforcement. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.3.2 Ensure workload namespaces have required NetworkPolicies defined

audit.command: Run the below command and review the NetworkPolicy objects created in the cluster. This command will list all namespaces in your OKE cluster that have one or more NetworkPolicy objects defined: echo -e "NAMESPACE\tNETWORKPOLICY_COUNT" && \ for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do count=$(kubectl get networkpolicy -n "$ns" --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' ') if [ "$count" -gt 0 ].

remediation.command: Follow the documentation and create NetworkPolicy objects as you need them. For OKE, define NetworkPolicies for workload namespaces based on the required allowed ingress and egress traffic, and confirm that the cluster uses a supported NetworkPolicy enforcement model. Clusters created with OKE use either the OCI CNI plugin or the flannel CNI plugin for pod networking, depending on the cluster network type and creation path. Oracle supports NetworkPolicy enforcement through Calico when using the OCI CNI plugin. Oracle does not support using the Calico network policy engine with the flannel CNI plugin. If the cluster uses the OCI CNI plugin, install and configure Calico network policy enforcement using Oracle’s documented process, then create the required namespace NetworkPolicies.

title: Apply securityContext controls to pods and containers
description: Apply Security Context to Your Pods and Containers. For OKE workloads, securityContext controls should be used with Pod Security Admission or an equivalent admission policy so pods and containers run with only the operating system privileges they require. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.5.2 Apply securityContext controls to pods and containers

audit.command: Review the pod definitions in your cluster and verify that you have security contexts defined as appropriate. Here is a key compliance check in OKE (Oracle Kubernetes Engine) to ensure all Pods define a securityContext at either the pod or container level: echo -e "NAMESPACE\tPOD\tHAS_POD_SECURITY_CONTEXT\tHAS_CONTAINER_SECURITY_CONTEXT" && \ kubectl get pods -A -o json \ | jq -r ' .items[] | .metadata.namespace as $ns | .metadata.name as $pod | (.spec.securityContext != null) as $hasPodSC | ([(.spec.containers[]?.securityContext != null)] | any) as $hasContainerSC | [$ns, $pod, ...

remediation.command: Use securityContext settings in workload manifests and enforce the required Pod Security Standard with Pod Security Admission or an equivalent admission policy. Avoid using legacy PodSecurityPolicy manifests for current OKE clusters. For normal application workloads, configure pod and container securityContext settings that align to the intended security level. Common settings include running as a non root user, disabling privilege escalation, dropping unnecessary Linux capabilities, restricting host namespace use, and setting read only root filesystems where the application supports it. securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true allowPrivilegeEscalation: false capabilities: drop: - ALL • Label workload namespaces to enforce the required Pod Security Standard.

title: Ensure image vulnerability scanning uses OCIR or a third party provider
description: Container image vulnerability scanning helps strengthen the security of OKE workloads by identifying known software weaknesses in the images those workloads run. This supports a more secure software supply chain and helps reduce the chance that vulnerable images are promoted into Kubernetes environments. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.1.1 Ensure image vulnerability scanning uses OCIR or a third party provider

audit.command: Verify that image vulnerability scanning is enabled for repositories that store images used by OKE workloads. For images stored in OCIR, review the Container Registry image scanner or OCI Vulnerability Scanning container scan targets and scan results. If a third party scanner is used instead, obtain equivalent evidence that images deployed to OKE are scanned and that findings are available for review. Checks the container scan targets in the compartment.

remediation.command: Enable image vulnerability scanning for OCIR repositories that supply container images to OKE workloads, or use an approved third party image scanning provider that produces equivalent vulnerability findings before image promotion and deployment. For OCIR, configure OCI Vulnerability Scanning with a container scan recipe and target for the repositories that store OKE images. Identify the OCIR repositories and compartments that provide images to OKE workloads. This establishes which repositories must be included in the scanning coverage. Configure OCI Vulnerability Scanning for the required repositories. Create a container image scan recipe in the compartment that will manage the scan configuration.

title: Restrict OKE and Kubernetes API access to required users
description: Restrict access to OKE and Kubernetes API operations to only authorized OCI IAM users, groups, and Kubernetes service accounts. Access should be limited based on the user’s required administrative, operational, or workload function. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.1.2 Restrict OKE and Kubernetes API access to required users

audit.command: For most operations on Kubernetes clusters created and managed by Container Engine for Kubernetes, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Identity and Access Management (IAM) provides access control. A user's permissions to access clusters comes from the groups to which they belong. The permissions for a group are defined by policies. Policies define what actions members of a group can perform, and in which compartments. Users can then access clusters and perform operations based on the policies set for the groups they are members of.

remediation.command: By default, users are not assigned any Kubernetes RBAC roles (or clusterroles) by default. So before attempting to create a new role (or clusterrole), you must be assigned an appropriately privileged role (or clusterrole). A number of such roles and clusterroles are always created by default, including the cluster-admin clusterrole (for a full list, see Default Roles and Role Bindings in the Kubernetes documentation). The cluster-admin clusterrole essentially confers super-user privileges. A user granted the cluster-admin clusterrole can perform any operation across all namespaces in a given cluster. Remove or reduce OCI IAM policies that grant unnecessary OKE permissions, and use Kubernetes RBAC roles and rolebindings to grant only the required Kubernetes API permissions inside the cluster. Avoid granting cluster-admin unless full cluster administration is required.

title: Restrict OCIR access for OKE workloads to required image pulls
description: Restricting OCIR access for OKE workload image pulls helps ensure that the identities used to retrieve workload images can pull required container images without also receiving broader registry visibility, push, delete, or repository management access. In OKE, this applies to the OCI IAM users, groups, cluster policies, and Kubernetes imagePullSecrets used to pull images from private OCIR repositories. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.1.3 Restrict OCIR access for OKE workloads to required image pulls

audit.command: Review the OCI IAM policies, OCIR repository access, and Kubernetes imagePullSecrets that apply to the identities used by OKE to pull images, and verify that those identities are limited to required image pull access. Focus on the OCI identity represented in the Docker registry secret, any OCI IAM policy that grants the cluster access to OCIR, and any repository policy or compartment policy that grants access to private OCIR repositories.

remediation.command: Enforce pull-only OCIR access for OKE workload image pull identities by limiting the OCI IAM users, groups, cluster policies, and imagePullSecrets used to retrieve private images. The runtime pull path should allow only the repository access required to pull image layers and manifests. Broader permissions that allow pushing images, deleting repositories, changing repository visibility, or managing repository metadata are not required just to start workloads. • Identify the OCI identities, groups, policies, and imagePullSecrets used by OKE workloads to pull private OCIR images. • Remove broader OCIR policies from runtime image pull identities. Avoid granting manage repos to identities that only need image pull access. • Replace broad repository access with read repos for the required repositories or compartments.

title: Allow only approved container registries for images used by OKE workloads
description: Allowing only approved container registries for images used by OKE workloads helps reduce supply chain risk by limiting where workloads can source their images. This creates a controlled image origin model in which clusters admit workloads only from trusted registries and can pair that control with OCIR image signature verification before containers are allowed to run. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.1.4 Allow only approved container registries for images used by OKE workloads

audit.command: Review the image sources currently used by the cluster and the admission controls that govern new deployments, then verify that workloads are limited to approved registries only. The strongest implementation for this control is an admission policy, because admission controllers can reject Kubernetes API requests before objects are persisted. For OCIR images, also review OKE image verification policy configuration where signed image enforcement is used. Include required Oracle managed image sources for platform components and add ons in the approved list.

remediation.command: Restrict OKE workloads to approved container registries by enforcing image source controls at admission time, rather than relying only on CI/CD checks or written standards. Enforcement can be implemented with an admission controller so image references are checked before the deployment is persisted. For OCIR images, use OKE image verification policies when signed image enforcement is required, so only images signed with approved OCI Vault keys are admitted. The approved registry list must also include the Oracle managed image sources required for platform components and add ons. • Include approved OCIR repositories, explicitly approved third party registries, and Oracle managed registries required for OKE platform components and add ons in the approved registry list. • Configure an admission control path so image registry source is checked before the workload is admitted.

title: Ensure Network Policy is Enabled and set as appropriate
description: Implementing Kubernetes NetworkPolicies in an Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE) cluster is a critical security measure for controlling and segregating Pod to Pod communication. By default, all pods in a Kubernetes cluster can freely communicate with each other, which increases the risk of lateral movement if a single workload is compromised. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.4.4 Ensure Network Policy is Enabled and set as appropriate

audit.command: Below is a command line statement to check whether NetworkPolicies are configured in your Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE) cluster: echo -e "NAMESPACE\tNETWORK_POLICY_COUNT" && \ for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do count=$(kubectl get networkpolicy -n "$ns" --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' ') echo -e "${ns}\t${count}" done Sample Output NAMESPACE NETWORK_POLICY_COUNT default 2 kube-node-lease 3 kube-public 5 kube-system 0 A count of 0 means no NetworkPolicy objects exist in that namespace and pods that are not selected by any NetworkPolicy ...

remediation.command: For OKE, do not use an isNetworkPolicyEnabled cluster flag. Configure NetworkPolicy enforcement by using a supported enforcement solution and then create the required Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources. If the cluster uses the OCI CNI plugin, install and configure the Calico network policy engine using Oracle’s documented process, then apply NetworkPolicy resources to workload namespaces. If the cluster uses flannel and NetworkPolicy enforcement is required, follow Oracle’s documented approach to replace flannel with Calico for new nodes, or create a replacement cluster design that supports the required policy enforcement. Do not install Calico alongside flannel. • Define namespace level NetworkPolicies after enforcement is available, and apply a restrictive default policy to each workload namespace where required.

title: Ensure the kubelet event recording QPS is set to an appropriate value
description: In OKE, this control is about tuning how quickly the kubelet records events so worker nodes capture useful operational data without generating unnecessary event volume. Oracle supports kubelet tuning for managed nodes through custom cloud-init initialization scripts and kubelet extra args, while worker node property changes are applied through node pool updates and replacement worker nodes. Reported as a manual review because it needs site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 3.2.6 Ensure the kubelet event recording QPS is set to an appropriate value

audit.command: To audit whether the kubelet event recording QPS is appropriately set on an OKE worker node, query the live effective kubelet configuration through the Kubernetes API server proxy and inspect the kubelet configz output for eventRecordQPS. Kubernetes identifies configz as the view of the kubelet’s final actuated configuration, and OKE managed node customization should be validated from the effective node configuration when kubelet settings are changed through cloud-init or kubelet extra args.

remediation.command: If the audit shows eventRecordQPS is set too low, the worker node may throttle useful event creation during burst conditions and should be adjusted. If the value is 0, Kubernetes defines that as no limit enforced, so it should be used only when the additional event volume is intentional and downstream capacity has been considered. If the field is missing or null, first confirm the configz response is complete, because Kubernetes identifies configz as the view of the kubelet’s final actuated configuration. In OKE, remediation should be made through the supported managed node initialization, node pool update, or node replacement workflow, not by directly editing the kubelet config file on the host, because Oracle supports custom cloud-init initialization scripts for managed nodes and applies updated worker node properties through new or replacement worker nodes.

title: Create administrative boundaries between resources using namespaces
description: Namespaces create administrative boundaries in OKE by dividing a cluster into logical partitions for teams, applications, or tenants. They are a core building block for multi tenancy, and several controls used to separate workloads, including quotas, network policies, and service accounts, apply to namespaces. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.5.1 Create administrative boundaries between resources using namespaces

audit.command: Verify that namespaces are present and are being used as intentional administrative boundaries for teams, applications, or environments in the OKE cluster. Namespaces are the core logical partition for multi tenancy, and they should be paired with namespace specific access controls and namespace level governance such as quotas, limits, and network policies. A namespace should be considered adequately administered only when it has a clear workload or team purpose, appropriately limited access, and the namespace level controls required for that use case.

remediation.command: Create separate namespaces for teams, applications, or environments that require their own administrative boundary, and move workloads out of the default namespace into that managed namespace structure. Make the namespace boundary meaningful by limiting access to the intended namespaces, applying namespace level governance such as quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies, and reducing broad cluster permissions that bypass the intended separation model. When stronger isolation is required for mutually untrusted workloads, use separate clusters rather than relying on namespaces alone. • Create dedicated namespaces for each team, application, or environment that needs its own administrative boundary. • Move user workloads out of the default namespace and into the appropriate managed namespaces.

title: The default namespace should not be used
description: Avoid placing application workloads in the default namespace, and instead deploy them into dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended team, application, or environment boundary. In OKE, namespaces are a primary logical partition for organizing workloads and supporting multi tenancy in a shared cluster. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Container Engine for Kubernetes (OKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.5.3 The default namespace should not be used

audit.command: Review the OKE cluster and verify that the default namespace is not being used for normal application administration or routine workload placement. Objects that do not explicitly specify a namespace are created in default, so the audit should confirm that teams, applications, and environments are instead using dedicated namespaces that align with namespace level access control, quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies.

remediation.command: Move user workloads out of the default namespace and place them in dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended team, application, or environment boundary. In OKE, namespaces are the core logical partition for multi tenancy, but they only become meaningful administrative boundaries when they are paired with namespace level access, service accounts, quotas, limits, and network policies. Because namespaced objects are created in default when no namespace is specified, remediation should address both existing workloads and the deployment process that created them there. • Create dedicated namespaces for each team, application, or environment that needs its own administrative boundary. • Move user workloads out of the default namespace and into the appropriate managed namespaces.
